you can also add control.inla=list(int.strategy='eb') which will help (a
lot).

for the weibull, you had several observations that were exactly 0, and
this cause a problem. I added small noise for those, as you see, and its
fine then.

I guess your $Status is 1 and 2, and this is what you want?  see
?inla.surv  normally, its 0 or 1, not 1 and 2, [different cencoring...].
please check.

there were also an issue with using improper prior for the intercept, so
I added prec=1 for the intercept and the fixed effects.

and better priors... Gamma(eps,eps) prior is very bad [I know, it have
been used a lot].

Hopefully, this will allow you to get started...

Best
H

messages.subject: How to handle complex replication schemes in INLA?
messages.subject_clean: How to handle complex replication schemes in INLA?
messages.body_plain:
Hello All,

In the data I am working with, most of the locations are unreplicated. However, for about a third of the locations, replication ranges from a single replication up to literally hundreds of replications. I'm building a model consisting of covariates and a gaussian spatial field with matern covariance. My questions are:

1) Can someone point me to an example of how to handle this? Most examples I see cover the case when locations have a shared number of replications, i.e. all locations have been replicated twice. There is gap between how I would imagine specifying it in the inla.spde.make.index/inla.spde.make.A functions and how these functions "know" which datapoint is a replicate for which location.

2) What would be the consequences, if any, of just ignoring the replication? In reading some of the literature, it seems it is more important to consider replication in the non-stationary case, but I'm not clear on this. I am not considering the non-stationary case at this time, though it might be unrealistic, if that simplifies things.

Regards,

Mark

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] How to handle complex replication schemes in INLA?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mark,

the answer depends on which model components take on different values
for the replicated observations.
In the simplest setting, the random spatial field component is the
same for all the observations, and it's only the measurement
likelihood model that takes different values.
If the random field component itself, for the whole spatial field, is
different, that's much more complex.

It sounds from your description that you're closer to the simpler
case, where each observation is linked to the spatial evaluation of a
single realisation of a spatial field, but with multiple observations
at some locations (with conditionally independent measurement noise).
In this case, there are two options you can use when calling
inla.spde.make.index and inla.spde.make.A:
For inla.spde.make.index, always just specify the information for the
the spatial field model size; if it's just a single fixed realisation
of the field, it doesn't matter how many observations there are, and
whether they are replicated or not.
For inla.spde.make.A, you have two choices, depending on how your data
is organised:
1) If your data.frame has one row per measurement, including the
location of each measurement, just provide that information to
inla.spde.make.A, with a coordinate matrix with one row per
measurement, inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc=youmeasurementlocations)
2) If your unique measurement locations are stored in a separate
structure, and your measurement data.frame has an "index" column
pointing to the location structure rows, indicating which location was
measured, then
you can supply that index information separately, via
inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc=uniquelocations,
index=measurementlocationindex)

If this type of model isn't what you have, we'll need more details of
the model structure.

Finn

messages.subject: Advice on calculating price elasticities
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have a large data set (daily sales data for 500 products over two years) and am trying to estimate price elasticities and cross-price elasticities. The end goal is to be able to estimate the volume that will be sold of all 500 products if I change the prices of multiple products. I am seeking advice please on how to best do this in INLA.

I would like to incorporate as much as possible of (1) the own-price elasticity for each product should be fairly similar (same types of product), (2) the products would all have a similar non-linear trend component, and (3) the cross-price elasticities should insignificant for almost all products (it's unreasonable to expect every product affects every other product).

If I weren't seeking to include cross-price elasticities, (1) and (2) are easy: I would create a random interaction effect between ProductID and price and simply add a non-linear term to the poisson model. The cross-price elasticities present a problem since there are so many coefficients (500 x 499 = ~250K) and material values are sparse. Even setting aside the number of coefficients, since I am fairly confident all of these products are substitutes I am fairly confident the coefficients are >= 0 and a normal prior might not be reasonable. Ideally I'd use something like a pc.prior, but my sense is that wouldn't be possible at this scale. I'd be okay with using a normal prior if necessary.

One last thought: I can use the units sold of the other products rather than the prices if it would be easier (i.e., I don't actually care about cross-price elasticities, I just need to understand how changing prices impacts other products).

Any thoughts would be very much appreciated. Thank you!

messages.subject: Simulate besagproper effect - gaussian likelihood
messages.body_plain:
Hi I am performing a simulation study and sometimes I am not recovering my besagproper precision parameter ( in some executions I can recover it but in others not).
Maybe could be a confusion between precision of the normal errors and the besag precision effects?

I attach my code, my code is similar to the one performed in inla.doc("besagproper") documentation but with a  covariate X.

graph = system.file("demodata/germany.graph", package="INLA")
g = inla.read.graph(graph)
## we will use replicated samples in our testing
nrep = 6
## make life easy; use dense matrix algebra
d = 1.0
tau = 1.0
Q = matrix(0, g$n, g$n)
diag(Q) = tau * (d + g$nnbs)
for(i in 1:g$n) {
  if (g$nnbs[i] > 0) {
    Q[i, g$nbs[[i]]] = -tau
    Q[g$nbs[[i]], i] = -tau
  }
}
R = chol(Q) ## 'chol' returns the upper triangular

b = c()
for(i in 1:nrep) {
  b = c(b, backsolve(R, rnorm(g$n)))
}
i = rep(1:g$n, nrep)

replicate = rep(1:nrep, each = g$n)

x=rnorm(nrep*g$n,0,1)

eta=1+x+b

y=rnorm(nrep*g$n,mean=eta,sd=1)

formula = y ~ 1 + x + f(i, model="besagproper", graph = graph,replicate=replicate,
                hyper = list(diag = list(param = c(1, 1))))
## use 'exact' observations, so we fix the noise precisin to a high
## value
r = inla(formula,
         data = data.frame(y, x=x, i,replicate),
         family = "gaussian")
summary(r)

Regards

- NA (non-spatial)
- 5
-10
-20
-30

- as resolution of the mesh gets finer, test MSE improves until 5, at which point test MSE gets worse.
- the CIs are always getting wider on the maps attached (far right images), but there is a considerable jump in width from 20 to 10

It seems there has been a violation of assumptions in my spatial term (matern/stationarity/isotropy), otherwise I don't see how it would be possible for the spatial term to "overfit." This leaves me with a challenging decision:

Pick model 10:
- Pro: best test MSE
- Con: massive CIs (pretty disappointing results for an interpretation perspective)

Pick model 20:
- Pro: small CIs and second best test MSE
- Con: Those CIs are, in my view, more theoretically invalid and therefore misleading

Or pick no model!

I would be curious to hear how other would choose.

Sincerely,

Mark

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

a few thoughts:

it's not clear how dense your observations are, but from the pictures
it seems they are relatively dense? Also, it's not clear what the size
of the study region is; the km numbers don't mean much in the absence
of that, and the typical distance between the observation sites.

With lots of data, the inference might simply be picking up that the
model isn't able to capture both long range behaviour/dependence as
well as short range behaviour/dependence, and therefore changes focus
depending on the mesh resolution

In this situation, the priors set for the dependence structure
parameters are likely to be important, so you should consider those
carefully (and make sure to use pcmatern, not matern).

One option is to add a second spatial field component to the model,
and set the two range priors differently for the two components, so
that one of them is "encouraged" to capture long range dependence, and
the other to capture short range dependence.

Instead of just looking at Squared Error and Credible Interval Widths
for the expectations, consider assessing data-level predictive
distributions instead; predictive log-score or similar would give an
overall assessment of the model prediction behaviour.
(for leave-one out predictions, the cpo calculations in inla already
provide one such diagnostic. For withheld test data, you'll likely
need to construct assessment code with the help of
inla.posterior.sample() )

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

inlabru separates "model components" from "predictor expressions", and
doesn't support the special "interaction operator *", but instead that
has to be coded explicitly.
For purely additive models, one can use the shortcut of only
specifying model components, which implies that the predictor should
be the sum of the components.

First, add a new column, anom_base =
anom_tmin_mar_may*base_tmin_mar_may to your data object.
Then the "interaction term" is just another ordinary covariate effect,
and the following should work:

bru(
  julian_lay ~ anom_tmin_mar_may + base_tmin_mar_may + anom_base +

site(map = coordinates, model = spde1),

 ...
)

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

as you clarified elsewhere this is for inlabru, and that the covariate
information is stored as two rasters, with one continuous and the
other (functionally) an 0/1 indicator.

First, convert the functionally 0/1 variable to actual 0/1 values, so
they can be used in calculations.
If these had been ordinary covariates, A and B,  stored in the data
object, you could have used
  A + B + AB(map = A*B, model="linear")
but as these are stored as rasters, that, as well as the following,
would _not_ work,
  A(map=A, model="linear") + B(map=B, model="linear") + AB(map=A*B,
model="linear")
since A*B as far as I know isn't defined for rasters in the way needed for this.

Instead, you can create a new raster, AB, that contains the pointwise
products of A and B, as a raster.
The last component is then + AB(map = AB, model="linear")

Alternatively, you could define a function fun(x, y) that evaluated
and returned the product of A and B at locations (x,y),
but the new raster approaches seems easier.

Finn

messages.subject_clean: How to calculate predictions for a linear combination in a model with an offset term?
messages.body_plain:
It is relatively straightforward to calculate predictions for a linear combination in a model without an offset term (see code below). However, I can't figure out how to calculate the same prediction for a model with an offset. The offset term doesn't get incorporated into a model.matrix object, and so I can't determine how to properly incorporate it into the linear combination. Thanks very much for your assistance!
   Judith

Reproducible code
# Artificial dataset of number of animals (N) captured in two sites (a, b) over time (2000-2004)
# The number of hours spent sampling (hrs) varies across years, and should be used as an offset
capture.dat <-   data.frame(N    = c(23, 20, 11, 15, 18, 28, 30, 23, 24, 22),
                            site = c(rep("a", 5), rep("b", 5)),
                            year = c(2000:2004, 2000:2004),
                            hrs  = c(5, 5, 3, 4, 5, 5, 5, 3, 4, 5))

# Fit basic Poisson model in INLA, without offset
mod.no.off <- inla(N ~ year + site,
                    data = capture.dat,
                    family = "poisson")

# Fit basic Poisson model in INLA, with offset
mod.w.off <- inla(N ~ year + site + offset(log(hrs)),
                    data = capture.dat,
                    family = "poisson")

# Now to predict the value for a linear combination that calculates the average across sites
# Manually create a dataframe that matches that output by model.matrix, but set the value for
# the factor variable equal to 0.5 to calculate the average
# Note I can't figure out how to provide a proper name for the intercept variable expect through
# this clunky method
predict.dat <- data.frame(intercept = 1, year = 2000:2005, siteb = 0.5)
names(predict.dat)[1] <- "(Intercept)"

# Convert to an inla.make.linkcombs object
lincomb.predict <- inla.make.lincombs(predict.dat)

# Extracting the predicted values for the linear combination is straightforward for the model
# without an intercept
predict.no.off <- inla(N ~ year + site,
                            data = capture.dat,
                            family = "poisson",
                            lincomb = lincomb.predict)
predict.no.off$summary.lincomb.derived

# But how to do so for the model with the offset?
# Assume that we want to predict the same linear combination as above, but with hrs fixed at 5
# If we naively proceed without adding the offset into the prediction
predict.w.off <- inla(N ~ year + site + offset(log(hrs)),
                            data = capture.dat,
                            family = "poisson",
                            lincomb = lincomb.predict)
# Then the predicted output is quite underestimated because the offset isn't included
predict.w.off$summary.lincomb.derived

s1 <- inla.stack(data=list(y =..., Ntrials =...),...)

messages.body_plain:
There are three ways to do this,

first is to use linear combinations, then if  'mu' have dimension m and
b have dimension k, the you need to define each one, like

lc1 = inla.make.lincomb(mu=1, b= 1)
names(lc1) = paste0("lc.1")

lc2 = inla.make.lincomb(mu=c(0,1), b= 1)
names(lc2) = paste0("lc.2")

etc,
where c(0,1), means 1*mu[2] ,and b=1, means 1*b[1]

and then join them together and add it to the call.

testit on a small example, before moving to the big one.

second, is to construct a fake linear predictor where you NA's out what
you do not need.

for this model

	eta = 0 + mu + b + eps_L

you will have a data.frame with idx.mu <http://idx.mu>, idx.b, and idx.epsL, say,

d = data.frame(y, idx.mu <http://idx.mu>, idx.b, idx.epsL)

just make a new one where you pad with NA (note that the data is also
NA'ed in this part)

na = rep(NA, length(y))

d.new <http://d.new> = data.frame(y=c(y,na), idx.y=rep(idx.y,2),
		idx.b= rep(idx.b,2),
		idx.epsL=c(idx.epsL, na))

in this way, the last half of the linear predictor, will contain the
linear combinations if mu+b

third, is to use inla.posterior.sample() and
inla.posterior.sample.eval()

r = inla(..., control.compute=list(config=TRUE))

xx = inla.posterior.sample(10000, r)

mu.b = inla.posterior.sample.eval(function() c(mu,b), xx)
## if these are the names... please fix

then each column will be a sample

messages.body_plain:
First off, thanks to the developers for all the work building R-INLA. I've found it to be really useful in my work. I am pretty new to this approach so forgive me if my question comes off as misinformed.

I'm trying to build a spatial model using grouped data (100+ groups) and would like to generate a prediction for any of the groups. From what I understand, I could create 100+ prediction stacks and combine them with the estimation stack and pass that to inla() as the data object. This seems expensive and I was wondering if it's possible to estimate the model using just the estimation stack, and run prediction after the model object is created? Any comments/guidance would be much appreciated, thanks!

Brian

Loc <- cbind(df$X, df$Y)
loc.domain <- expand.grid(-15:15, 15:45)
Mesh1 <- inla.mesh.2d(loc.domain=loc.domain, cutoff=6,
                      offset=c(6,9),
                      max.edge = c(6, 9))

A_point <- inla.spde.make.A(Mesh1, loc=Loc,
                            group=groups,
                            group.mesh=inla.mesh.1d(groups, degree=0),
                            n.group=n_groups)

spde1 <- inla.spde2.matern(Mesh1, alpha = 2, constr=TRUE)

s.index <- inla.spde.make.index(name="spatial.field1",
                                n.spde=spde1$n.spde,
                                n.group=n_groups)

stack.est <- inla.stack(data=list(y=df$response),
                        A=list(A_point),
                        effects=list(c(s.index,
                                       list(intercept=1)
                        )
                        ), tag="est")

formula_p1 <- y ~ -1 + intercept +
  f(spatial.field1, model = spde1, group=spatial.field1.group,
    control.group=list(model='rw1', scale.model=TRUE)
  )
######
# I could create 100+ of these and combine them with stack.est into join.stack
######
group_1 <- 1
A_pred <- inla.spde.make.A(Mesh1, loc=as.matrix(pred.grid),
                           group=rep(group_1, nrow(pred.grid)),
                           n.group=n_groups)

stack.pred.response <- inla.stack(data=list(y=NA),
                                  A=list(A_pred),
                                  effects=list(c(s.index, list(intercept=1))), tag="pred")

join.stack <- inla.stack(stack.est, stack.pred.response)

join.output.1 <- inla(formula_p1, data=inla.stack.data(join.stack), family='binomial', Ntrials=1,
                    control.family=list(link='logit'),
                    control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(join.stack), compute=TRUE, link=c(1)),
                    control.compute = list(dic = TRUE),
                    verbose=TRUE
)

######
# Can I create just the estimated model and run prediction after?
######

join.output.2 <- inla(formula_p1, data=inla.stack.data(stack.est), family='binomial', Ntrials=1,
                    control.family=list(link='logit'),
                    control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stack.est), compute=TRUE, link=c(1)),
                    control.compute = list(dic = TRUE),
                    verbose=TRUE
)

Hi,
That sentence should be rewritten!

For this kind of situation, one can use inla.posterior.sample() to sample from the model components, which then allows computing any type of prediction via Monte Carlo estimates (averages of the samples for expectations and variances, and quantiles for posterior quantiles, etc). messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I would extract the entire model component that includes _all_ the
groups for the field; it's one single latent component, full_field.
Then call inla.spde.make.A with the mesh, and the desired loc and
group combinations;
  A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc=prediction_locations, group=prediction_group)
Then A%*%full_field should be the evaluated field for each row of
  cbind(prediction_locations, prediction_group)

I try to avoid the direct indexing as much as possible, and use the
available wrapper functions like inla.spde.make.A to do the work for
me.

Finn

> > Hi again,
> >
> > I've made a quick version of a mesh-to-Spatial* conversion function,
> > inla.mesh2sp. See code below.
> > It outputs SpatialPolygonsDataFrame (for the triangles) and
> > SpatialPoints (for just the vertices).
> > Including a special object for just the domain polygon is harder, but
> > we have internal code in the
> > 'excursions' package that I could covert to work with this new function.
> > Is this the sort of thing you had in mind? Can you give it a try and
> > send me comments, and then I'll add it to the package.
> >
> > Finn
> >
> > #' Convert inla.mesh to sp objects
> > #'
> > #' @param mesh An \code{\link{inla.mesh}} object
> > #' @return A list with \code{sp} objects for triangles and vertices:
> > #' \describe{
> > #'   \item{triangles}{\code{SpatialPolygonsDataFrame} object with the
> > triangles in
> > #'   the same order as in the original mesh, but each triangle looping through
> > #'   the vertices in clockwise order (\code{sp} standard) instead of
> > #'   counterclockwise order (\code{inla.mesh} standard). The \code{data.frame}
> > #'   contains the vertex indices for each triangle, which is needed to link to
> > #'   functions defined on the vertices of the triangulation.
> > #'   \item{vertices}{\code{SpatialPoints} object with the vertex coordinates,
> > #'   in the same order as in the original mesh.}
> > #' }
> > #' @export
> > inla.mesh2sp <- function(mesh) {
> >   crs <- inla.CRS(inla.CRSargs(mesh$crs))
> >   isgeocentric <- identical(inla.as.list.CRS(crs)[["proj"]], "geocent")
> >   if (isgeocentric || (mesh$manifold == "S2")) {
> >     stop(paste0(
> >       "'sp' doesn't support storing polygons in geocentric coordinates.\n",
> >       "Convert to a map projection with inla.spTransform() before
> > calling inla.mesh2sp()."))
> >   }
> >
> >   triangles <- SpatialPolygonsDataFrame(
> >     Sr = SpatialPolygons(lapply(
> >       1:nrow(mesh$graph$tv),
> >       function(x) {
> >         tv <- mesh$graph$tv[x, , drop = TRUE]
> >         Polygons(list(Polygon(mesh$loc[tv[c(1, 3, 2, 1)],
> >                                        1:2,
> >                                        drop = FALSE])),
> >                  ID = x)
> >       }
> >     ),
> >     proj4string = crs
> >     ),
> >     data = as.data.frame(mesh$graph$tv[, c(1, 3, 2), drop = FALSE]),
> >     match.ID = FALSE
> >   )
> >   vertices <- SpatialPoints(mesh$loc[, 1:2, drop = FALSE], proj4string = crs)
> >
> >   list(triangles = triangles, vertices = vertices)
> > }
